utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, Colonel, is still in force. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I asked you yesterday to make a pause after my question, and I will do so after your answer, and it would be good for us to do that today as well, because of an accurate interpretation and the transcript. Yesterday you told us something about the documents at the command of OG South, the war diary, the record or log-book of orders received, and also the briefing book. So what I would like to know is who controlled the entry of data in all of these records?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff and the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And was it the main task of the Chief of Staff to take care of the accuracy of the documents being maintained by the command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My learned friend and I showed you some documents, some orders from the 1st Military District and orders from OG South, so would you agree with me that the commander of OG South, after he received orders from his superior command, and after they were processed at the OG South command, did he transfer then all of those orders into his own orders, orders of the OG South, which he then transferred to, or conveyed to his units?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. About 80 to 90 per cent of such orders were then passed on to subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In view of this percentage would you agree with me that all the important key orders were then drafted as orders of OG South?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I think that perhaps it would be fair to look at Exhibit 429 again. I assume that yesterday you were tired when you were making that diagram, so I wanted to ask you something. That's the diagram of the command post. This is just to clarify any uncertainties. Thank you. For the sake of clarity, what I would like you -- what I would like to ask you is the following: The way you've sketched this, it looks as if you directly went from one room to another. Was there any kind of passage or corridor there?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a corridor between the operations room and these other rooms. I apologise, but after 15 years I really cannot be so sure about the sketch of the desks, the chairs, the rooms. I dropped the corridor, but I didn't do it on purpose. I was tired, you're right. I was tired, so that's why I didn't indicate where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's why I thought it would be good to come back to this question so that perhaps we could clarify some things. Could you please tell us, this descent into the lower rooms or at the lower level, was that at the end of the corridor; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably that's how it was. It would seem that the way down led from the corridor. I'm not really precise, Mr. Vasic. In this case I cannot be precise. This is on the basis of my recollection, so it's more or less like that. There was a corridor, the entrance was from the corridor leading down, yes. I remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And did you enter all the other rooms from a corridor, the operations room on one side and then on the other side, the left side, all the others?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not the operations room, but the entrance to the other rooms was from the corridor. The operations room was entered directly from the street, from the porch, and then there were the auxiliary buildings where the generators were that served the staff command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you first, could you indicate where this corridor was on the diagram?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these offices and the working rooms, I could erase that and I could say that the corridor was about one metre wide, so I could extend this by one line and that's what that looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like some instructions from you. If we add the corridor on this diagram, I'm afraid then that we won't be able to see anything. So is it necessary to redraw the diagram anew, or can we just make an annex to it and keep the annex under the same exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, to answer your question, I need to know what use you need to make of it. At the moment the evidence is clear that this is a sketch, that it is inaccurate, that there is a corridor between the operations rooms and the smaller rooms to the top of the diagram, that the entrance to downstairs is at the end of the corridor, and there is also an entrance to those rooms in the corridor. Unless you need to have some precise marking of something for some other purpose, I don't think you need to alter this at all. The evidence is all there on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for that instruction. So I will not dwell on this diagram anymore. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, can we now look at some entries of the war diary, this is Exhibit 401, and I would like to ask you to find the entry for the 4th of October, 1991, at 12.00. This is on page 12 of the English version, and page -- have you found it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you didn't tell me the page number. Could you please give me the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: 4th of October at 12.00. I'm trying to find it in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 4th of October. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 12.00. Could you please read what it states there?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I was looking at the English translation, and I think there is a mistake in the date with this entry, let me just check. But you can read this entry, this was of the 4th of October at 1145.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The commander of the OG South issued an order to Lukic Branislav to immediately or directly command and coordinate all activities in the axis of attack of the 2nd Assault Detachment." And this is number 2020/1173 to the command of the 453rd Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic Branislav is the person we mentioned already who took over the command of the 2nd Assault Detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To immediately command and coordinate all activities along the axis of attack of the 2nd Assault Detachment. That's what was stated and that's what I noted down. The document was registered at the command of the brigade. 453rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the entry for the 8th of October? At 2310 hours, and in English that is page 18. And for you that's the page ending with 452; that's the ERN number. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please read it out?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Colonel Dr. Vuk Obradovic called and asked if the Ustasha units were surrendering and how many had surrendered. He requested that the commander of the OG South be told that on the 9th of October he was working according to his plan (the original decision) regardless of the situation and conduct of the Ustashas. "We should not count on major air force support."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the commander was informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And can you see on the basis of this entry that Vuk Obradovic had frequent contacts by telephone with the OG South command, as a unit that it sent -- that sent daily reports out very frequently?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please now look at the entry for October 9th at 8.00? This is page 19 in the English, and in your copy, Witness, it's page ending with 453.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you kindly read it?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The commander of the 1st Military District arrived at the OG South group command and ordered the OG South to hold the belt area from the River Vuka to the Danube. He specified the areas of responsibility and gave information on the remaining units of the 1st Military District. He had information on the state of the infantry in the area of responsibility of the 1st Military District."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So could it be concluded on the basis of this entry that on the October -- on October 9th it was specified that the operations zone of OG South, in the north up to River Vuka and the River Danube, and that on the 18th of November OG South was only then ordered to cross the bridges and to occupy the rest of the town?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't bring any documents which would regulate this. He came the day after the guards brigade commander was appointed as commander of OG South, and it says here that he was informed of the situation and that he informed the command about the situation in the field. At that point this was a specific task to hold the strip from the Vuka River to the Danube, that's what was orally said to him. I don't know, I mean he had the plan which was then specifically developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, do you remember whether the orders for combat operations of OG South were in line with what we're talking about now, that it was the assignment of the unit -- that the assignment of the units was split into two stages, the second stage of which was to get to the River Vuka?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Phase two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that it was phase two.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you would like us to go back to the decisions from that period, that's what it specifically says. The first stage would be to reach such-and-such a point, and then the second stage would be to reach such-and-such a point. We could go into that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we please now go to Exhibit 410? Would you please blow it up a little? Thank you very much. This is a decision to extend the attack. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that on the screen. I haven't found it -- among my documents in the binder that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is a decision by Operations Group South dated the 29th of October, 1991, to extend the operation in Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Item 1 says: "I hereby decide."

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 1: "I hereby decide to simultaneously and energetically use all forces with the air force support and artillery support and to infiltrate some forces to extend the attack along the entire front line. The main axis of the attack will be along Sajmiste Street-Dalmatinska Street-Alija Alijagica Street and the republic square. The auxiliary axis will be at Vucedol (Mala Dubrava) and the neighbourhood of Mitnica with the following objective: "At stage 1 of the operation, take control of the neighbourhood of Mitnica and cut it off from the rest of the town, take control of the neighbourhood of the 6th Proleterske Divizije, and the part of town near the streets of Ognjena Price and Alija Alijagica. After that, at stage 2 of the operation, reach the River Vuka and the River Danube. "Operations disposition or operative disposition: Five assault detachments ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Based on this order, can we agree that stage 2, which was the final stage of this operation, was to reach the banks of the Vuka and the Danube?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that follows unequivocally from the commander's decision, doesn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can we know please go to 401, Exhibit 401? This is the war diary. And can you please find the entry in reference to the 10th of October, 7.00. For the benefit of my learned friends, the page number in English is 20. I assume you have found it already sir, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 0700 hours, the 10th of October, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please read that entry for us?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We received an order by the command of the 1st Military District to set up check-points to check the flow of food and medicines organised by the Republic of Croatia for civilians in Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that this order by the 1st Military District ordered the setting up of a check-point to monitor the food and medicine convoy so that no weapons, ammunition or explosives entered the town of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I think that is precisely what the order states.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps also remember that once the convoy was checked it should be allowed to smoothly enter Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The order was quite precise. The convoy was to be let through, and the supplies were to be distributed to the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday by my learned friend about the convoy, about that note in that report saying that the JNA units from the barracks were in no position to guarantee the safety of a convoy in Croatian territory under the control of the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the report you mean, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Bearing all this in mind, what I want to know is, do you perhaps remember what the real problem was? Perhaps the real problem was that the Croatian forces refused to open up their lines and remove their obstacles, separating them from the JNA units. They simply refused to let the convoy through, and that was the real reason why the convoy didn't go on and reach the centre of Vukovar eventually?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that the reasons were precisely the ones that I stated in my report. But I think what you are suggesting is true, roughly speaking. There is something I wrote in my report that is related to this particular difficulty, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. What you wrote in your report is logical and suggests that the JNA units were in no position to guarantee the security of the convoy in the territory held by the Croatian forces. Would that seem to be a fair inference?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that much is certain. There is no doubt about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please go back to the war diary, Exhibit 401, and go to the 17th of October at 6.30. The page reference is 27 for the English.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 17th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The 17th of October, 6.30.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please read that out for us?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Order strictly confidential No. 1614-82." I think Skoric is the one who made this entry. So it's a little difficult for me to make out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The English says the 16th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair enough. The order states that: "... despite the enormous losses suffered by the Ustasha forces they are still opening heavy artillery fire, also from the areas of the villages of Ilok ..." There's something just before Ilok, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, could the speakers please kindly be asked to speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "... and Sotin. The Ustashas withdrew in groups and fled to the woods, especially on the right bank of the Danube between Opatovac and Jakubovac. The Danube between Opatovac and Jakubovac. Therefore " -- I can't read this. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could the speakers kindly be asked to speak one at a time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You keep speaking in as the witness is speaking, and the interpreter can't hear both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I will try to take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said you couldn't read this, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'll try to read this, and you check whether that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: "It was therefore ordered that command of the 12th Corps and the 1st Proletarian Guards Motorised Division from all command posts ..."

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That in all, yes, right. Can I do this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That they should set up command posts in all the villages?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you look at this order by the 1st Military District, does it not seem that it outlines actions that should be taken against the Croatian forces in Ilok and Sotin? Those Croatian units firing at JNA units sometime around mid-October 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I look at the substance, that is not my assessment of what it means. Secondly, as far as I know, the operations group command never received an assignment like this in any of the orders received. Not at any point in time, throughout the Vukovar operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So this assignment is in reference to members of the 12th Corps and the 1st Proletarian Guards Motorised Division, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my understanding of this particular entry in reference to the order from the 1st Military District. If you have the specific order, perhaps I might be able to interpret it more closely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: A brief objection, Your Honour. Or intervention, as Mr. Vasic would put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just in relation to the transcript, at page 10, line 12, I think the -- there's been a translation error as it was being read out what the diary contained, the entry in the diary. And the entry in the diary states that despite enormous losses the Ustasha forces suffered they're still resisting heavy artillery attacks, and in the transcript it's read that they are still opening heavy artillery fire. That that was the witness's answer. But it seems to be a misreading of the diary entry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic, you've heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have taken note, Your Honour. Perhaps we can ask the witness to read this again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I think the witness read exactly what went down in the transcript. But let us please go back to the 17th of October, 6.30. Would you please be so kind as to read out the first segment again, because that's what the objection is about. Can you please do that again for us?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll certainly do my best. I'll probably do better now, as opposed to the first time around. "Order strictly confidential number 1614-82/dated the 16th of October, 1991." The order states that: "Despite the enormous losses suffered by the Ustasha forces they are still resisting heavy artillery attacks." End of segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've got that cleared up now. Can we please go back to the 19th of October? It says between 01 and 10.30. For my learned friends' reference, page 28. Have you got that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that means --

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. 0030, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: 19th of October, 0100 to 1030?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, the next entry, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next one is 0100 to 1030. Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The Ustasha forces are opening artillery fire on the Vukovar barracks sector."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This entry must have been based on the report you received from the Vukovar barracks, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was probably received by the operations duty officer. I suppose I wasn't there myself. He just made a note in his notebook, and probably he told me the next morning about that particular entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may as well have been there. It's possible. But the way information was entered into the war diary, the technical aspects, as far as the times when I wasn't there was concerned when one of the duty officers was there, it was done like this, but that was night-time only, because over the day all the operatives were there, and we were the ones entering all the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've explained that already. I just meant to stop you to ask you this: Is it your conclusion that perhaps it was the duty operations officer that took this down, given the time of the entry?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. It's possible that the duty operations officer told me the next morning, and then I made an entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please -- we're still with this exhibit, and I would like to have the page marked as 0293-5446 run up on the screen, if possible, please. 0293-5446. That's what we were looking for at the beginning, it's the entry for the 4th of October, but the English translation seems to contain a confusion about these two dates, so I couldn't find the B/C/S reference. I have provided the B/C/S page, so this is in relation to 1200 hours. For the benefit of my learned friends, it's page 12 in English. Have you found that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. The date, the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the war diary, the date is the 4th of October at 1200 hours.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not 12, it's 1145, I'm not sure what you mean. 4th of October. The authorisation by Colonel Bojat, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The page that is on the screen. Can you see that page? It's the next entry on that page.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my document there is a page missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I think it was just put together in the wrong way, and that was the reason that I took so long to find it.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my apologies then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The page number is, the last digits are 446. It's the second entry. You have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have it on the screen, 446. Yes, right. It's right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please read that out for us?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1200 hours, 1100 hours, 1200 hours. "Reconnaissance organs of the 1st Motorised Battalion report that there is an Ustasha headquarters underground in the old and new hospitals."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You made this entry based on a report you received from someone in the 1st Motorised Battalion, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the note says: "All command bodies have been informed."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, could you please now go to the 19th of November, 1400 hours. For my learned friend, page 41.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 19th of October?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The 19th of November, 1400 hours.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1314, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind, sir?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The command of OG South was informed that the Ustasha authorities refused to take in a convoy comprising 16 buses carrying civilians that had been sent to Zupanja. These were sent back to the area of responsibility of OG South."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is this reference to that same convoy carrying civilians on their way out of Vukovar and then returned by the Croatian authorities who refused to have them, which is what you testified in chief yesterday?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it appears to be in reference to. We sent reports to our superior command, and I outlined the situation in a more detailed manner. I referenced all the check-points and the specific times when the buses were sent back. But they refused to have them. And it was like that over the three days. The situation did not change. So this information is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the returns of the convoys posed great problems to the command of OG South because they needed to be secured, people fed and accommodated, and moved across the territory as well as establishing new rules -- new routes to exchange them?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will leave aside the war diary for a moment. I wanted to ask you something about the functioning of the command. We saw from the war diary that there was telephone communication with the chef de cabinet of the SSNO, Mr. Vuk Obradovic, and I suppose there were other telephone connections with the command of the 1st Military District. I'm interested in knowing where were such reports recorded, the ones that were received via telephone from the 1st Military District and the SSNO, and the reports sent by the command of OG South to these superior commands. Where were such reports recorded?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be quite precise. In that part of the communications centre, there was Major Tatic there and two warrant officers as well. They would take those phone calls, depending on who it was that was sending their report, and taking into account the importance of such a telephone call, the matters were regulated the following way: If it came from the cabinet of the commander or Chief of Staff, or the head of the operations organ, and provided none of those people were there, the chef de cabinet, if information was such degree that wasn't deemed of utmost urgency, it was then transferred later and conveyed to the people who were supposed to know of that. Otherwise, if any of those people were present there, they would take the phone call. Usually entries were not made if calls were made from the 1st Military District. Rather, if matters were urgent, we would try to find the right officer who would take that information down. When it comes to the subordinates who sent out reports, they used codes. At the communications centre there was a form which the radio man would have to fill out by using the code book. But some of the conversations were not coded either. The person reporting had to state the person to whom that should be transmitted, be it the commander or someone else, and the radio man was supposed to do that. He had his own notebook where he kept his notes, I told this to Trifunovic, I told that to Mrksic, and so on and so forth. This is the way communication went, because the dynamics of the situation in the operations room was such that at a given time some of the officers would be there, and they could take phone calls. I'm not talking about the way of sending out coded messages, but just I'm explaining the phone calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Any such information received on the phone, be it from the superior command or one of the subordinate units, any important order or information would be taken down the way you explained by the people who were tasked with communications at the command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was important information and the Chief of Staff or commander were not there, all they asked -- the person calling would only ask when would such-and-such person be there, and then they would call later. Because something -- some of the documents and orders were strictly confidential and were not to be told to the radio man but only to the commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: During your testimony in chief, when you read out the report of OG South command for the 19th of November, we saw that there was mention of local commanders assigned by the commander there. And you stated that based on that document, for Ovcara, Jakubovac and Grabovo, Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic was appointed, and you said that he was appointed on the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please refer me back to the document to see which date exactly. When it comes to the change of command inside a certain area, the commander would also appoint a new commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 418, tab 27. What we are interested in is on page 2 of the report with ERN number 0467-2870. This is the report of the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Therefore, on this page, in item 3 it states that village of Ovcara, village of Jakubovac, village of Grabovo Lieutenant-Colonel Misovic, Slobodan would be appointed commander and upon his departure from the zone of responsibility. So Lieutenant-Colonel Slobodan Misovic and upon his departure from the zone of responsibility of OG South, Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic, Milorad was appointed?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was appointed by an order, and this is a report, and if -- you can see for yourself it's not a particularly clear report. It was drafted poorly by the operative. So this was just reporting on the order of his command, of his appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Since this report encompasses the period between the 18th of November at 6.00 p.m. Until the 19th at 6.00 p.m., it covers 24 hours. Is it possible that Mr. Vojnovic had been appointed commander on the 18th, particularly having in mind that on the 18th of November his unit in that area was securing the captured members of the Mitnica brigade? Therefore, my question is: Could it be that this order appointing him the local commander was made on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was appointed on the 20th, since the date on the order is the 20th. Maybe I drafted the order on the 19th for the 20th, and as it is stated in the report, it says that he will be appointed. Yes, on the 20th at 6.00 the order was issued appointing Vojnovic commander. Perhaps he ordered that I draft that in the evening on the 19th. He said put it in the report that Vojnovic will be appointed and draft the order appointing him. The order is on the 20th at 6.00. And we can then assess that that was the time when he received the order and that was the time of effective appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what the number of the order is?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the number of the order. I made a note in -- during the proofing. That order concerns itself with local commanders within the area of responsibility and that they should take full responsibility for the affairs pursuant to the order of the 19th. It could be the 19th. I apologise. Maybe it was drafted on the 19th. I can't find it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I need to be fair, and I have to put it to you that the 20th Partisan Brigade in the areas of Jakubovac, Ovcara and Grabovo withdrew on the 17th of November, and I put it to you that the area was taken over by the 80th Motorised Brigade on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Maybe they were told this orally, and then the order followed on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you said that they may have been ordered orally on the 18th, and that he received the order on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. And I found it in one of my notes that it was drafted on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After the 16th of November, do you remember that the 80th Motorised Brigade, and I have in mind the period between the 16th and the 20th of November, by orders of the commander of OG South, the Stara Pazova TO detachment was resubordinated to the 80th Brigade, as well as the unit from the 40, 400 -- 44th brigade [as interpreted] as well as the tactical group of the 95th Motorised Brigade. It seems I will have to repeat to have it recorded for the transcript. The armoured battalion of the 544th Motorised Brigade and the tactical group of the 195th Motorised Brigade were resubordinated to carry out tasks in the area of Ovcara, Jakubovac and Grabovo; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly what units were resubordinated to the 80th. I only remember the armoured battalion. And it didn't take place in a single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, as I said, it lasted more than one day. That is, between the 16th and the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember they were being reinforced. That is that the commander resubordinated certain units. I don't remember which exactly. But that could be easily established, based on the notes or orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we please see on the screen 65 ter number 577, ERN for the B/C/S 0327-1247, and for the English 0327-1247. 0327-1247, yes. Can you see it on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This is an order. Could you please read it out for us?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Regulating the issue of resubordination - Order: In order to unify the command for the forthcoming actions, resubordinate: The armoured battalion of the 544th [as interpreted] Motorised Brigade to the 80th Motorised Brigade. All issues pertaining to resubordination will be regulated by the command of the 80th Motorised Brigade." Item 2: "Until a new task will be issued, the armoured battalion of the 544th Motorised Brigade will carry out its tasks in keeping with the decision of the 16th of November, 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you also state the date of the order?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 8.00 on the 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would I like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received. Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It has been tendered, Your Honour. It's exhibit number 420.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that at a tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, tab 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, and I thank my learned friend for his assistance. Could we have Exhibit 372 shown on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, Mr. Vasic would make it much easier for everyone in the courtroom should he refer to the tab numbers used previously by Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I don't know whether you heard that. You did?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just to help, Your Honour. This document doesn't have a tab number, but it relates to a previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Smith. That is correct. We've tendered this document with the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, do you have that document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, can we read there that the tactical group of the 195th Motorised Brigade is being resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade on the 19th of November at 1800 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 800 hours.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This tactical group, was it resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade to secure the area of Ovcara, Jakubovac and Grabovo, as well as to be prepared to mop up the terrain in the area of Mala Dubrava forest and the settlement of Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By order of the operations group, it was clearly defined. These were the tasks assigned, and in item 3 in the forthcoming actions other tasks are specified to be received by the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade. I believe that is sufficiently clear. Therefore, the commander had to carry out these tasks. As for some others, well, he could decide on his own on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the tactical group numbered over 450 troops?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the figure is there between 350 and 450, including all the detachments and groups that were coming in. Therefore, I may conclude that this one was no exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If we also have in mind the armoured battalion mentioned a minute ago, would the figure then amount to around 1.000 soldiers being resubordinated to the 80th Motorised Brigade in the last three or four days?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we have in mind the tactical group and the battalion, then that figure is not as high. I don't know what other units were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The TO detachment of Stara Pazova?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the figure is right, because an armoured battalion can have up to 300 or 400 troops, plus the other units, it could be as many as 1100.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday in your testimony in chief you mentioned a group of security officers who came in the evening of the 19th to Negoslavci. You said they briefly met with the commander. Could you confirm to us that the encounter was so short that they were not even offered any coffee?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't have any coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Then you said they went to Vukovar, and you never saw them afterwards; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I know a lot of time passed, and that it's not easy to remember, but who was your duty operations officer on the 18th, 19th and the 20th of November, 1991? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is impossible for me to remember that. Even when such things are defined by daily orders, at that time we would take turns or we would replace each other if there was any need to do so. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it is difficult to remember after 15 years. Do you remember whether on the 19th of November you were in the operations room for as long as the commander was there? Rather, my question is: Did you leave after he did on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they came on the 19th, and when they were sent to go to Vukovar, I was there. When I went to take a rest, well, I don't know. I don't know whether I left after the commander had, because then at 2000 hours the duty operations officer was there, and that all the officers from various units came in, and tasks could be carried out, new assignments issued, and then people could take their rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the morning of the 20th, were you at the command post?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was always there in the morning, as early at 7.00 or 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was the commander in the operations room with you on the 20th, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And in the morning and in the course of the day, he didn't leave the command post and the operations room?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He didn't go out until lunch. Perhaps out in the terrace a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Until lunch, you say. Is that the time that you mentioned yesterday that in the late afternoon or towards the evening he went to the logistics base in Berak?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I remained behind to draw the map and make the calculations, and all the attachments to the map, and the commander went out. I don't know what time it was, 1600 hours, 1700 hours, it was November, it was already dark at that time. When he came back, he didn't tell me where he was coming from, and I didn't ask him. But I find -- found out from the senior officers that he was either in the medical facilities or in Berak. He could have only been to those two places.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And you said that he returned sometime after midnight?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After midnight. I had already completed the map. Colonel Pavkovic was with me until about 11.00 and then he went somewhere, and I stayed behind to wait for the commander, because of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also replied to a question by my learned friend that you heard that Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic had come to the command sometime between 21 and 2200 hours?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I did hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In view of what you said a little bit earlier, he could not have met Colonel Mrksic because at the time, as you said, you heard that Colonel Mrksic was at Berak and not at the command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I heard was that he wanted to meet the colonel, the commander. But I don't know whether he did manage to see him or not. I really didn't find that out. I wasn't interested in the reasons why he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But from what you say, the commander was not at the command post at that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not in the operations room in Negoslavci. Perhaps he was in a neighbouring house somewhere there, or he was there for some time and then he went down there. I don't know what his movements were. Once he left the operations room, I didn't follow where he was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But according to what you said that you heard, he wasn't there, he was either at the medical facility or at Berak?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time I think he was not there at the premises that I had made a diagram of.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you heard that at that time he was either at the medical facility or at the command post in Berak?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So he was not at the command post that you sketched, and he could not have met Lieutenant-Colonel Vojnovic there. That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: My objection is that the witness has stated earlier that he was told that he was at the command post -- sorry, at Berak or at the medical centre, but he wasn't sure where he was. He said he may have been outside of the command post, and I just -- such questions are just asking for speculation on the witness's behalf, and I'm not sure whether they're that useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, I must state my client's position in relation to his movements on the 20th of November. He claims that after the regular meeting at the command in the afternoon he went to Belgrade on the 20th of November, 1991 in order to prepare for a meeting with the federal secretary that was held on the 21st of November, 1991 in the morning. And he was not in Negoslavci in the evening of the 20th of November. What would you say to this assertion by my client? I am obliged to state his defence.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I am sticking to an entry in the war diary that he left in the morning at 8.15 on the 21st. My exact recollection, though, is that he left in the morning and that the night before I was working on the map. That means that he could have left on the 18th also if that is what it states in -- in the war diary. I assert that I made entries in the war diary in a responsible way, and when I look back those two facts indicate to me that on the 20th he was there, because the night before the departure I was busy with these things that I told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And what would your comment be if I were to tell you that possibly you have mistaken the dates and that perhaps you worked on the map on the 23rd of November in order for him to go to see General Zivota Panic at the 1st Military District command on the 24th, and it was not for the 20th and the 21st, because there was a protocol reception at the federal secretary's at that time. There was no briefing. Secondly, on the 20th Colonel Pavkovic was accompanying or escorting the convoy for Sremska Mitrovica, so he wasn't in Negoslavci. So is there a possibility that you are perhaps mistaken about the dates that you worked on the map?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not have mistaken the dates of my work on the map, because I was working on information for such an important briefing. The entry in the war diary, and you know that I constantly asked myself if it was possible that I had made a mistake or that I slipped and made an erroneous record, but everything to date indicates that this wasn't so. As for all the events, I recall them because I go back one by one, so this is logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we please look at Exhibit 401; this is the war diary. So could we look at the entry for the 21st of November at 8.00. For my learned friends, this is page 41 of the English. The B/C/S version, that's on the last page. Would you please read the entry for the 21st of November, at 8.15?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The commander of OG South and a group of officers went to a reception by the federal secretary in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So based on this entry, you could say that the commander and some other officers went at the same time to Belgrade for the meeting with the federal secretary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of this entry, you could conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in view of the time of the entry, the time of the departure, on the 21st of November, 8.15, could you tell us how the commander left for Belgrade, what means of transport did he use?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he went by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this the same topic, Mr. Vasic, or are you moving to something different?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that your question comes at the right moment. I am moving to a new topic, so perhaps it would be better if we were to take our break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume at five minutes to 11.00. That's a slightly longer break than usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So let us pick up from where we left off before the break. On the subject of the topic we covered just before the break, the departure of the commander for Belgrade, could we please look at Exhibit 422. That's the order of the resubordination of Mr. Trifunovic dated the 21st of November, 1991, which you discussed yesterday with my learned friends. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It helps the interpreters in particular, Mr. Vasic. It may be 21. 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, that comes at the exact moment. It's tab 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think it's a brief intervention, Your Honour, it's resubordination order of Colonel Mrksic, not Mr. Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a mistake in the interpretation. Obviously I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, yesterday you said in response to a question by my learned friend that this order was probably signed by Chief of Staff who was Lieutenant-Colonel Miodrag Panic at that time.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The order was issued at 6.00 in the morning on the 21st of November, 1991; is that correct? Could you please confirm whether in the rules of military service in the rules of brigades it states that the commander signs orders, especially of this importance?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does it not also state in the rules of service, the rules for brigades says that -- say that the Chief of Staff would sign instead of the commander only when the commander is not at the location, and because of the urgency, they cannot wait for him to return. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we then conclude that the Chief of Staff, Miodrag Panic, signed this document because the commander was not at the command post at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Vasic, could have been signed at 10.00 also. It was drafted at 0600 hours, and in practice you do not go to see the commander that very instant the man is perhaps doing something else. You don't knock on the door and say, here, sign this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But you didn't answer my question whether when the Chief of Staff signed this document the commander was not at the command post at the time. That's what I wanted to know. But what you have just said of course is implied.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps he was. But if he had gone on the 21st, as I seem to recollect on the bases of the entry in the war diary, perhaps he was in a hurry and did not sign it at the moment that the document was prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But if we look at the rules of service, the Chief of Staff can sign a document only if the commander is not at the location, if he's not present?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Perhaps he signed it when the commander was there, and perhaps he signed it after he had gone. Somebody, in that case, violated the rules of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now that we are looking at this document, I would just like to ask you something about the contents of this document and the terms that are used. Is this text of the document that you say you drafted something that was actually copied from the text of the order of the 1st Military District which you said you had received and on the basis of which you said you drafted this order?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It states here on the basis of the newly arisen situation and the order of the 1st Military District. Had it been exclusively ordered on the basis of the order of the 1st Military District, it would have said on the basis of the order of the 1st Military District. But it says, "Further to the newly arisen situation and the order of the 1st Military District." What the newly arisen situation was, I cannot really tell you at this moment, but there is the order by the 1st Military District somewhere here. But I think that I did write it quite precisely, and it wouldn't have been signed if it wasn't quite precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that you drafted this order on the basis of the contents of the order that you received? That was my question. So are the terms that are used in the order that we're talking about terms that were also in the order by the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them probably were. Some of them were used because of the situation that was there at that particular time, and it was suggested to me that I should insert that. I don't know whether this was done by the chief or the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking about the terms Seseljevci and Sumadinac [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This term Seseljevci, Seselj's men, since the term for Leva Supoderica was something that was known in the command that that detachment was there, so perhaps the typist put the term there and we didn't notice it. Perhaps I used that term because I was writing quickly. So I just happened to use that term. But I explained which detachment that actually was. It could be a technical mistake, a typo as a result of -- everybody knows what that would be a result of. In the military, a poor operations officer would receive poor grades.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Another thing about this order, it refers to an order of the 1st Military District, strictly confidential No. 115-151, dated the 20th of November, 1991. I'm not sure whether you ever saw this document of the 1st Military District, the one numbered 115-151?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I probably answered this while I was testifying in chief these days. We've gone through all the documents. I'm not sure if this was one of them. Do you want me to go back to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I still haven't received the translation, unfortunately. I'm referring to this 1st Military District document, and I have informed my learned friends accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Just in relation to this document, that's correct. We haven't received the translation for this one. We've been provided a large number of documents and we've received all of the others. So that the Prosecution can follow this discussion, I'm wondering whether either this discussion about this document be put off until we receive the translation; or, alternatively, perhaps I can discuss it further with the witness in re-examination. But it's -- we wouldn't be able to agree to its admission until -- until we receive the translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the cross-examination is likely to be able to be adequately dealt with at the moment without a translation. But if it's important, re-examination on the document can be delayed until a translation is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think the actual situation we end up with may be simpler. I want to know only about two aspects of this document; the first being the date, and the second being what it really shows. And I think we can stop right there as far as my cross-examination is concerned. I just want to show the witness this document, he can read the date for us, and the heading of the document. If the usher could please hand the witness a copy. The document is 0D00-0343. It's been scanned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I assume this may take a while. I mean for you to have a look before we can continue.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will not be asking you about any details. All I want to know is whether this is a 1st Military District document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please just tell us what this document is about, the heading?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a report or, rather, information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So this is no order?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's no order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would that imply that you could not possibly have drafted the order on the resubordination of Operations Group South, Exhibit 422, 464-1, based on this?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This might be a technical error, when it reads order and not informational report. I would need to go through this to see if any resubordination issues are referred to or ordered. This may be about certificates being issued, people signing off and payments being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please have a look, then? I wasn't going to go further with this, since there is no English translation and my learned friends don't have the privilege of insight into this particular document. But please, can you just go through it briefly and see if you can answer my question.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it. This information or report contains no reference to issues previously regulated by the brigade commander's order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to explain what I think about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please, by all means, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that there was a different order that was issued on the same day, and that arrived on the same day as this information report. Probably as it was being processed the number of this information report was copied instead of the order number. So it must be a mere technical error.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll no longer be consulting this report. But let me ask you this: Do you remember that regular combat report in relation to the 21st of November and signed by the Chief of Staff, Miodrag Panic? Does it not state that resubordination was based on the 1st Military District order 115-151? So it's the same mistake recurring in all these reports being forwarded to the 1st Military District, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This order was written at the same time, and the number of this order, or of this information report to the superior command -- it was probably right there on the table, and when the report was produced the same number was used. I suppose I don't need to explain what a mountain of paperwork the officer who was drafting this document was facing on his table, so errors were certainly possible. But I may as well ask the following question: Why didn't the person reading this notice? However, such errors do happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: There's something else I would like to ask you about this order, something you were asked yesterday by my learned friend. You told him that all these units mentioned in the order, I'm referring to Exhibit 422, the order on the resubordination of Operations Group South, the one produced by Operations Group South, all the units mentioned there remained within the composition until the 21st of November. My question is: Shouldn't a unit remain within the composition of its superior unit until it is formally resubordinated to a different unit? This could have been by midnight, between the 21st and 22nd of November, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, resubordination of units from other larger units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I don't wish to interrupt. But Exhibit 422 is not an order, it's a report, and the witness may clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 422, isn't that the order on the resubordination, 464-1?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Bear with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Smith, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry. Exhibit 422 is tab number 31, and that relates to a combat report. Sorry, and Your Honour, I've -- I believe we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Smith, it is a document that in its own terms describes itself as an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trifunovic, let us now go back to this previous issue. If those units arrived earlier pursuant to the resubordination order, had they not then by this time left Operations Group South in terms of being part of their establishment or overall composition, their resubordination means that they ceased to be part of that unit?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't think I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'll try to rephrase. While testifying in chief yesterday you said that the units mentioned in Exhibit 422 in this order were under the command of OG South until the end of the 21st of November, 1991, which means until midnight. What I'm asking you is: Based on this order, would it not seem that they left Operations Group South earlier on, at the moment they were originally resubordinated and sent to their new units based on this order, the ones that they were now resubordinated to?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The superior commander had to specify the time when these units were to leave and join someone else. A dead-line must also be provided for any such steps to be taken within the order, so that resubordination can be prepared and so that any units may reach their eventual destination, the unit that they're being resubordinated to, so that may account for the time-lag.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I do understand that. The dead-line is the last dead-line set by the commander, right? But if the units came earlier, they were resubordinated earlier, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that means nothing. They still have full responsibility until the dead-lines set by the superior commander. They might as well have dealt with the same caboodle in just two hours. But the responsibility rests with the commander receiving these units, and his responsibility starts at the time specified by the superior command. These dead-lines are sometimes unrealistic. Sometimes things can't be done fast enough, so there need to be other steps taken, and sometimes they are realistic, but sometimes it can take up to two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let's try to look at the language and the phrasing of the order. It says that resubordination should be carried out during the 21st of November and not by the end of the 21st of November.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the course of the day, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Day and night, by 2400 hours, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If this means by 2400 hours, then it would probably say by the end of that particular day, the 21st. And it says the 21st, until such time as the unit was ready to join the unit to which it was subordinated?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both civilian and military terminologies, you know what a dead-line means when a dead-line is set for the same day. That means the end of that particular day, which is midnight. And this is always implied. It is not necessarily stated explicitly. Otherwise, it could have said something like by 2200 hours, by way of an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Something else about the order and about the signature, or the Chief of Staff, the person you've told us about. Yesterday, while testifying in chief, you said this order may have been signed by Miodrag Panic. What I want to know is: If the commander wasn't there and the Chief of Staff, Miodrag Panic, was standing in for him, what would his responsibility have been during that time?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, that largely depends on any assignments left by the commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: He is standing in for the commander, so what sort of assignments could the commander previously have given him?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having been authorised by the commander, the only person who can set assignments to the units is the Chief of Staff. A commander leaves the area; before he leaves, he authorises the Chief of Staff. And in terms of this authorisation, he could have given any sort of assignment at all, conceivably. Unless there were no limitations imposed by the commander, these could have been any assignments, in terms of their potential nature. However, commanders do usually set certain limitations, and for this reason it's very difficult for me to comment more incisively.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If the range of assignments had been unlimited in terms of what had been ordered by the commander, would he have had the same kind and degree of responsibility as the commander then?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You remember looking at that set of instructions. Well, there is a commander who fails to set down the assignments in writing for the benefit of whoever is standing in for him. Then the commander must bear responsibility for any situations that may arise. He may be on leave, he may be on a leave of absence, whatever. But that changes nothing about the principle. If indeed that is the case, then this should be the answer to your question, shouldn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the Chief of Staff in terms of establishment, is he the Deputy Commander regardless of any written orders that may or may not be left behind?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Under the rules in the commander's absence, unless ordered otherwise, should he not stand in for the commander in all the different segments of command?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. As for the issue of responsibility, that is not something that I can necessarily determine. Under the general principles, the commander bears all responsibility. The principles say nothing about him not being responsible when he is being temporarily replaced by the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps if you can remember something pertaining to the 20th of November, could you tell me whether you saw at the command post someone from the cabinet of the federal secretary or Colonel Coric or Colonel Loncar or Colonel Abramovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th Colonel Coric, I don't think he was there only on the 20th, he came on several occasions. As for the others, I don't remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for trying to remember. Could we please have Exhibit 370 shown? And I wanted to ask you something concerning that. It's not in the binder. It is an exhibit that was introduced through another witness. Thank you. Mr. Trifunovic, on the screen before you there is a document entitled "Command of the 1st Military District, highly confidential 1614-162 dated the 16th of November, 1991." And it represents the overview of the composition of the forces sent to the first directorate of the General Staff by the Chief of Staff of the 1st Military District, Lieutenant-General Stojanovic. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we see a page of this document, bearing the number of 0345-0009, being the second page of the document? Thank you. Since you were tasked with some specific tasks inside the staff, could you tell us whether you remember the following: In column 3, the units of OG South should be represented, including those that fell under the OG South establishment, as well as the resubordinated units. This overview of the units of OG South, is that a true reflection of the situation until the 16th of November?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because it is dated the 16th.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we scroll down. A bit further down. That's good.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But now I can't see the whole thing, the whole page. Perhaps I can read when I see the entire page. Well, maybe you could zoom in a little, because I saw the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In order to be of assistance, I could ask the usher to provide you with a hard copy. It should make it easier for you.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it well now. Thank you. Yes. It is almost clear to me concerning the overview of the units within Operations Group South, but I'm unclear as to the BGs, the fighting or combat groups 1, 2 and 3. They must have been formed from some of the above units. Therefore, what is below them shouldn't be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see, what you are talking about is the river navy and we're not interested in it right now. It's the navy.

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As for the Guards Motorised Brigade within OG South, the 2nd Armoured Battalion, the 2nd Military Police Battalion, the LSAD PVO, HAD 155, it was never part of the guards brigade; that is not correct. If we are talking about the establishment, this must have been attached at a later point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This represents the composition put together by the Chief of Staff of the 1st Military District reflecting the situation on the 16th of November, 1991. I believe this includes the units that fell under OG South and in -- under establishment and the attached units?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says OG South, the guards brigade, and its units. That's what I'm trying to explain. Then the 20th Partisan, with its units; then the 80th Motorised and its units; the armoured one with its units; the sabotage detachment of the 93rd Protection Regiment and its units. As far as the Guards Motorised Brigade, that is completely incorrect. It's got going to do with anything. It is correct that the 20th had three partisan battalions, the 80th Brigade, the 1st Engineering, the 1st MTB, then the LAD PVO, and I believe they had a military police company. The armoured, just one battalion, that's fine. The sabotage detachment, the 1st Sabotage Detachment with a battalion of the military police minus one company. And the river navy was never part of OG South. You can see the form for yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. You told us that as regards the other units, everything is okay. But what's wrong with the Guards Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following things: The second was within the armoured unit, yes. The 2nd Battalion of the military police, that is okay. The LSAD PVO, that's fine. The AJD 155, it was never part of the guards brigade. HAD 105, the rear battalion, AJD 122, it says they came from the 453rd, but it states here that those were units of the guards brigade. That is incorrect. And where can we find the 1st Guards Battalion? Where is the 1st Battalion of the military police? This overview is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? If we see the Guards Motorised Brigade and what it says there, two motorised battalion, one armoured battalion, two military police battalions?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are fine. I didn't see the full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As for the units that didn't belong to the guards brigade, as you say, it says here the 155th, then 105/80, meaning they came from the 80th Brigade, and 122 out of the 453rd Brigade. Were those the reinforcements attached to the Guards Motorised Brigade once it entered OG South?

utterances.speaker: RADOJE TRIFUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those units were attached, but so was the 20th Partisan Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
